newsitem.title: USA: Harlyn may seek bankruptcy protection.
newsitem.headline: Harlyn may seek bankruptcy protection.

text.p: Harlyn Products Inc said it is experiencing liquidity problems and may need to seek Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection.

In a statement issued late Tuesday, the special order jewelry company also said its auditors had resigned late last month and the American Stock Exchange has begun procedures to delist the company's stock.
The company also said chairman and founder, Harold Weisbrod has returned to the position of chief executive officer. The position has been vacant since late last year, when William Hood resigned.

Due in large part to a 30 percent decline in sales and substantial writeoffs of inventory and other assets in excess of $8.5 million, the company said it recorded a loss of $14.5 million or $3.06 a share on sales of $25.9 million for the year ended June 30, compared with a loss of $1.87 million or $0.39 a share on sales of $36 million for the prior fiscal year.

For the three months ended June 30, the company recorded a loss of $6.9 million or $1.45 a share on sales of $5.4 million, reflecting a 38 percent decline in sales and inventory write downs in excess of $4.5 million. In the year-ago period the company reported a loss of $2.97 million or $0.62 a share on sales of $8.7 million.

As a result of the losses and writedowns, the company said it is experiencing liquidity problems and is currently attempting to negotiate an extension of its bank borrowing agreement that terminated October 1 and its agreement with its gold lessor, which has expired.

The company said it is hopeful about renegotiating both agreements; however if it were unsuccessful, the company would be forced to consider the possibility of restructuring its debts under the protection of Chapter 11 of the Bankruptcy Code.

In other matters, the company said the company's independent auditors, Deloitte & Touche, resigned on September 27, prompting the company to delay filing its annual 10K report with the Securities and Exchange Commission. The company said it is in the process of retaining new auditors.

The company also reported it has signed a definitive agreement with L.L. Knickerbocker to buy all the stock of its Harlyn international Thailand subsidiary and the company is also negotiating for the possible sale of its domestic operation with several domestic companies.
Both transactions are conditional and no assurances can be made that either transaction will be completed.
In an interview, Weisbrod said the moves are part of an effort to "downsize" Harlyn to its core business. He said there may be some layoffs but the cuts would not be drastic.
The company also revised operating results for the quarters ended December 31, 1995 and March 31, 1996 due to a miscalculation of leased gold in its Thailand facility.
The effect of the revisions are to change previously reported profits of $128,000 or $0.03 per share for the three months ended December 31, 1995 to a loss of $697,000 or $0.15 a share.
The loss for the six months ended December 31, 1995 was revised from $762,000 or $0.16 a share to a loss of $1,587,000 or $0.33 a share.

For the three months ended March 31, 1996, the effect of the revisions was to change the loss of $6,640,000 or $1.40 a share to a loss of $6,032,000 or $1.27 a share. For the nine months ended, the loss was revised to $7,619,000 or $1.60 a share previously reported to $7,402,000 or $1.56 a share.
